449.title: The seven oft-repeated
449.hook: We gave you seven oft-repeated verses and the great Qur'an, taken as the Fatiha (15:87)
449.howItsDone: Muslims recite al-Fatiha in every unit of every prayer, and also at weddings, over the sick and in memory of the dead; teachers cite 15:87–88 to remind students that the Fatiha is a treasure that makes envy of others' wealth unnecessary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, adh-dhikr, the Reminder God promised to guard, to a mocked Prophet. Your line was it is guarded. What did you give a better place, and how did the small care feel? Day four hundred forty-nine.

A companion named Abu Sa'id ibn al-Mu'alla was praying in the mosque in Medina when the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ called his name. He didn't answer until he'd finished. The Prophet reminded him, gently, that the Qur'an tells believers to answer God and His messenger when they're called. Then he said: before you leave this mosque, I'll teach you the greatest surah in the Qur'an. He took his hand. They walked toward the door. And Abu Sa'id, worried the moment would pass, said: you told me you'd teach me. What the Prophet said at the door is in Bukhari.

The Prophet said: alhamdu lillahi rabbil 'alamin. It is the seven oft-repeated, and the great Qur'an that I was given. He was pointing to al-Hijr, verse eighty-seven, which Pickthall translates: "We have given thee seven of the oft-repeated (verses) and the great Qur'an." At the start of this year, we stood back and looked at the Fatiha whole, and at what happens to words said in every prayer. Today, look at what the verse calls it: a gift. And look at the very next verse, because that's where al-Hijr takes it. Verse eighty-eight, in paraphrase: so don't strain your eyes toward what We've given some of them to enjoy, and don't grieve over them, and lower your wing in tenderness for the believers. Commentators read the two verses together. You've been handed seven verses and the great Qur'an. Don't stare longingly at other people's wealth. You're not the poor one in the room. Al-Hijr is counted among the Meccan surahs, from years when the believers had little power and the powerful had plenty. The verse tells them what they're holding. Another hadith, in Muslim's collection, has an angel telling the Prophet: rejoice in two lights given to you that were given to no prophet before you, the Opening of the Book and the closing verses of al-Baqarah. So the Fatiha is mathani, folded and repeated, and it's also a treasure in the hand of someone who may have very little else. Every time it's said, the gift is opened again.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: recite the Fatiha slowly. If you know it, say it in your head, one verse per breath, in Arabic or in English, as if you were opening something given to you. If you don't, hold just its first words: praise be to God, Lord of the worlds, one phrase per breath. And if your mind drifts to something someone else has that you don't, notice it, and come back to the words. The bell holds the time.
As-sab' al-mathani. The Fatiha's seven verses, folded and repeated in every prayer, called a gift in Surah al-Hijr.
Your line: seven, repeated. Today, the next time you catch yourself envying what someone else has, name one thing you've already been given. Day four hundred forty-nine.

450.title: Until certainty comes
450.hook: worship your Lord until certainty comes to you (15:99)
450.howItsDone: Muslim scholars teach 15:99 as a call to keep up worship for the whole of life, reading al-yaqin as death, and they cite it against the idea that a person who reaches certainty may abandon the prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, as-sab' al-mathani, the seven oft-repeated, the Fatiha as a gift. Your line was seven, repeated. When envy came, what did you name that you'd already been given? Day four hundred fifty.

Here's a pattern people describe. Someone starts a practice: praying, reading, sitting each morning. For a while it glows. Then it doesn't. They're going through the motions, and a voice says: if you're not sure anymore, why keep doing it? Wait until you feel it again. Surah al-Hijr ends with a verse that sounds, at first, like it agrees. Worship your Lord until certainty comes to you. Until you're sure. Some people have read it exactly that way. Commentators like Ibn Kathir say that reading gets it backwards.

First, where the verse comes from. Verse ninety-seven, in paraphrase: We know your chest is tight because of what they say. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is being mocked in Mecca. And God's answer, in verses ninety-eight and ninety-nine, isn't argument. It's practice. Glorify your Lord with praise, be among those who bow down. And then, in Pickthall's translation: "And serve thy Lord till the Inevitable cometh unto thee." Pickthall says the Inevitable. The Arabic word is al-yaqin, certainty, the certain thing. And commentators such as Ibn Kathir say the certain thing here is death, the one event no one doubts. They point to a scene in Bukhari. When a companion, 'Uthman ibn Maz'un, died, the Prophet said of him: as for him, al-yaqin has come to him. Certainty, meaning death. So the verse doesn't say worship until you feel sure, then stop. It says keep worshiping for as long as you live. Ibn Kathir, for one, rejects the reading that a person who reaches certainty can drop the prayer; the Prophet himself prayed until the end of his life. Yaqin, as a word, still matters a great deal. The Qur'an speaks of knowledge of certainty, the eye of certainty, the truth of certainty, and later Sufi writers built a ladder of faith from those phrases. But the verse puts the practice first, not the feeling. You don't wait for the glow to come back before you show up. You show up, and keep showing up, until the one certain thing arrives. The verse measures a practice in a lifetime, not a mood.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep a practice without waiting to feel sure. This one. Right now. Maybe today you feel close, maybe you feel nothing at all. Either way, sit, and breathe. Don't check how it feels. Just do the two minutes, the way you'd brush your teeth on a day you didn't feel like it. If you pray, you can say subhanallah with each breath. If your mind wanders, come back. Showing up is the whole practice today. The bell holds the time.
Yaqin. Certainty, the certain thing. In 15:99, commentators read it as death: keep worshiping until it comes. Today's word.
Your line: until the certain thing comes. Today, do one daily practice even if you don't feel like it, and notice that you did it anyway. Day four hundred fifty.

451.title: Countless favors
451.hook: if you counted Allah's favors you could not number them (16:18)
451.howItsDone: Muslims recite 16:18 and 14:34 as reminders of God's favors, and many teachers have students list blessings to see the list break down, answering with alhamdulillah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, yaqin, the last verse of al-Hijr, and your line was until the certain thing comes. Did you keep one practice going on a day you didn't feel like it? Day four hundred fifty-one.

Surah sixteen is called an-Nahl, the Bee, after a few verses near its middle. But some early scholars gave it another name: the surah of favors. Read the opening and you'll see why. It reads like an inventory. Cattle, for warmth, for food, and, the verse adds, for beauty, when you bring them home in the evening and drive them out in the morning. Horses and mules to ride, and as an adornment. Rain to drink, and for the pastures. Stars to steer by at night. The sea, with fresh fish and things to wear. Then, after the list, the surah stops counting.

Verse eighteen, in Pickthall's translation: "And if ye would count the favour of Allah ye cannot reckon it. Lo! Allah is indeed Forgiving, Merciful." The word is ni'mah, a favor, a blessing, a grace. Notice something some commentators point out: it's singular. If you tried to count the favor of God, not the favors, you couldn't. Take one: your breath. It depends on lungs, on air, on a planet with the right mix of gases, on the night you slept through without thinking about it once. One favor opens into a thousand. Now, there's an almost identical verse in Surah Ibrahim, which we read last week, verse thirty-four. Same opening: if you counted God's favor, you couldn't number it. But it ends differently: truly, man is unjust, ungrateful. Here, in an-Nahl, it ends: truly, God is forgiving, merciful. Commentators have long noticed the pair. One verse looks at what people do with the favors: they forget, they waste them, they take them as owed. The other looks at what God does in return: forgives, and keeps giving anyway. You can't count the favors, and you can't count the times they went unthanked, and both verses say so. The surah's list isn't meant to be finished. It's meant to break down. You start counting cattle and rain, and somewhere around the stars, you realize the counting is hopeless. That moment, when the list fails, is the point. Last week we read: if you give thanks, I will give you more. Today: you couldn't count them if you tried.
screen: `NI'MAH — A FAVOR, A GRACE.` · `SINGULAR: EVEN ONE IS ENDLESS.` · `14:34 — MAN IS UNGRATEFUL.` · `16:18 — GOD FORGIVES.` · then, large: `UNCOUNTABLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: try to count, and stop. Sit, and breathe. Start counting favors, one per breath. Your breath itself. The floor holding you. Light. Water. Someone who knows your name. Keep going. Somewhere along the way, the list will start to feel endless, or you'll lose count. When it does, stop counting, and just sit inside the part you can't number. If you pray, you can say alhamdulillah there. The bell holds the time.
Ni'mah. A favor, a blessing, a grace. In 16:18, even one favor of God is too many to count. Today's word.
Your line: uncountable. Today, start a list of favors on your phone, add to it whenever one occurs to you, and leave it unfinished on purpose. Day four hundred fifty-one.

452.title: Milk between
452.hook: from between waste and blood, pure milk, pleasant to drink (16:66)
452.howItsDone: Muslims commonly say bismillah before eating or drinking and alhamdulillah after, and some follow the Prophet's teaching to ask for blessing when given milk; 16:66 is often cited when speaking of everyday gifts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ni'mah: a favor, a gift, and your line was uncountable. Did you start counting favors and give up somewhere? What number did you reach? Day four hundred fifty-two.

A glass of milk on a kitchen table at night. It's about the plainest thing in the house. It goes into tea, into coffee, into a child's cereal, and nobody asks where it was made. An-Nahl, the surah of the bee, has been listing gifts since its opening: rain, cattle, date palms, grapes, the stars you steer by. And in the middle of that list it stops at the plainest drink there is, points at the inside of an animal, and says: look where this came from.

Pickthall translates the verse, 16:66, like this: "And lo! in the cattle there is a lesson for you." Then: "We give you to drink of that which is in their bellies, from betwixt the refuse and the blood, pure milk palatable to the drinkers." Start with the word lesson. In Arabic it's 'ibrah, from a root that means to cross over. A lesson, in this sense, is something you cross from: you look at one thing and arrive somewhere else. The verse wants you to cross from a glass of milk to the One who gave it. Now the picture. The verse names two things nobody wants to drink, waste and blood, and then, between them, something you'd hand to a child. Two words describe it. Khalis: pure, unmixed. It shares a root with ikhlas, sincerity, the name of Surah 112. And sa'igh: easy to swallow, going down without a struggle. Notice what the verse doesn't do. It gives no lecture on how milk is made. Classical commentators wrote about it with what they knew in their day, but the verse itself only says: this is a lesson, and here is your drink. Milk mattered in the Prophet's life. A hadith in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi says the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ taught that whoever is given milk should ask God to bless it for them and give them more of it, and said he knew nothing else that served as both food and drink. So the verse lands on something people actually lived on. And it hands you a way to see. A lot of what's good in a life came out from between things you'd never choose: a friendship from a terrible job, patience from a long illness, a recipe from a lean year. The verse doesn't say the waste and blood were good. It says something pure came out from between them.
screen: `A LESSON: 'IBRAH, TO CROSS OVER.` · `BETWEEN WASTE AND BLOOD.` · `KHALIS: PURE. SA'IGH: EASY TO DRINK.` · `GOOD THAT CAME FROM BETWEEN.` · then, large: `PURE MILK PALATABLE TO THE DRINKERS.`

segments.voice: If there's a drink near you, milk, tea, water, anything, take it in your hands. Before the first sip, think back along its road: the animal or the cloud, the field, the truck, the person who stocked the shelf. Muslim custom is to say bismillah before drinking and alhamdulillah after; if you pray, you can do the same. Take one slow sip and hold it a moment. Notice how easily it goes down. That's the verse's word. Then sit with the cup in your hands and let the thanks stay quiet. The bell holds the time.
Milk between. Pure milk, easy to drink, brought out from between waste and blood: a lesson in the plainest drink in the house. Today's word.
Your line: pure from between. Today, notice one good thing that came out of a messy stretch of your life, and name it to yourself, without pretending the mess was nice. Day four hundred fifty-two.

453.title: The bee
453.hook: your Lord inspired the bee to build, to eat, to make honey with healing in it (16:68–69)
453.howItsDone: Some Muslim households keep honey as a remedy and cite 16:69 and the hadith of the man with the stomach complaint; the bee verses are often recited and taught to children as a sign in creation.

segments.voice: Yesterday: milk between, pure milk from between waste and blood. Your line was pure from between. Did you find one good thing that grew out of a mess? Day four hundred fifty-three.

Somewhere a jar of honey is sitting on a kitchen shelf. It is the work of a crowd you'll never meet, flying back and forth over fields you'll never see. This surah, number sixteen, is named after that crowd. An-Nahl: the Bee. Of all the creatures in its long list of gifts, the bee is the one that gets the name on the cover, and two verses all its own. Today, those two verses.

Verse sixty-eight begins, in Pickthall's words: "And thy Lord inspired the bee". The verb is awha, from the same root as wahy, the word for revelation. It's the word used when God speaks to prophets. It's also used, elsewhere in the Qur'an, for the quiet prompting given to the mother of Musa. And here it's used for an insect. Commentators usually explain it as instinct, a guidance placed inside the creature, but they keep the word: the bee is guided. Then come three instructions. Make your homes in the hills, in the trees, and in what people build for you. Eat from every kind of fruit. And follow the ways of your Lord, made smooth for you. Arabic grammarians point out that these commands are in the feminine form. Then verse sixty-nine: from their bellies comes a drink of many colors, with healing in it for people. Many colors: anyone who's seen pale clover honey next to dark buckwheat knows it. Healing for people. The verse ends: this is a sign for people who reflect. There's a story in Sahih al-Bukhari that shows how seriously the companions took it. A man came to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and said his brother's stomach was troubling him. Give him honey, the Prophet said. The man came back: no better. Honey, again. Back again, no better. Honey, a third time. When the man returned once more, the Prophet said, God has spoken the truth and your brother's stomach is wrong; give him honey. He did, and his brother recovered. Muslims read the verse as a sign, and some also keep honey in the kitchen as a remedy. The verse names it a healing, not the only one.

segments.voice: If you have honey in the house, put a little on a spoon. If you don't, anything sweet will do, or just remember the taste. Before it touches your tongue, look at its color, light or dark, one of honey's many colors. Taste it slowly. Let it sit. Then, for the rest of the sit, think of one thing in your life that heals you: a person, a walk, a song, a habit. If you pray, you can say alhamdulillah for it. The bell holds the time.
The bee. Guided by the same word as revelation, told to build, eat and follow smooth paths, and giving a drink of many colors with healing in it. Today's word.
Your line: healing in it. Today, notice one small thing that does you good, a cup of tea, a friend's voice, ten minutes outside, and let yourself receive it fully. Day four hundred fifty-three.

454.title: Justice, excellence, giving to kin
454.hook: Allah commands justice, excellence and giving to kin (16:90), recited in many Friday sermons
454.howItsDone: In many mosques the imam recites 16:90 at the end of the Friday sermon before the prayer begins; Muslims cite it as a summary of social ethics and give charity to relatives as both charity and keeping family ties.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bee, guided to build and eat and make a drink of many colors. Your line was healing in it. What did you notice that did you good? Day four hundred fifty-four.

If you've ever sat through a Friday prayer in a mosque, you may have heard this verse without knowing its number. In mosques from Cairo to Chicago, imams often close the second half of the sermon with it, just before the call to stand for prayer. Week after week, the same few lines. A tradition says this custom goes back to the Umayyad ruler Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz. Whatever the sermon was about, the week ends on these words. Today: the verse the sermon comes home to.

Pickthall translates it: "Lo! Allah enjoineth justice and kindness, and giving to kinsfolk, and forbiddeth lewdness and abomination and wickedness. He exhorteth you in order that ye may take heed." Three things commanded, three forbidden. Look at the three commanded. First, 'adl: justice. The root carries the sense of balance, of making two sides level, the way a scale settles. Justice is giving each person what is due to them, no more and no less, including the people you don't like. Second, ihsan. Pickthall says kindness; others say excellence, or doing what is beautiful. In a famous hadith, the angel Jibril asks the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ what ihsan is, and he answers: to worship God as though you see Him, and if you don't see Him, He sees you. So ihsan is justice with something added: doing more than what's owed, and doing it well, as if someone were watching who matters. Third, giving to kin. Not giving in general, though the Qur'an asks for that too. Giving to the near ones, the relatives. Notice the order: the scale, then the extra, then the people closest to you, who are often the hardest to be fair to. A saying attributed to the companion Ibn Mas'ud calls this the most comprehensive verse in the Qur'an for good and for evil. And a hadith in Tirmidhi says charity to a relative counts twice: once as charity, once as keeping the family tie. Then the three forbidden: shameful acts, munkar, what is known to be wrong, and baghy, overstepping against others. The verse closes not with a threat but with a reason: He counsels you, so that you might remember.
screen: `THREE COMMANDED, THREE FORBIDDEN.` · `'ADL: THE LEVEL SCALE.` · `IHSAN: AS IF YOU SEE HIM.` · `GIVING TO THE NEAR ONES.` · then, large: `JUSTICE, EXCELLENCE, KIN.`

segments.voice: The practice is to give something to a relative. Sit, and let your breathing slow. Picture your family, the whole loose circle of it: parents, siblings, cousins, an aunt you haven't called in a year. Let one face come forward. What could you give them this week? It could be money if they need it, but it could also be time, a meal, a message, a fair hearing in an old argument. Choose one. If you pray, you can ask for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Justice. 'Adl, the level scale, first of three things the verse commands, followed by excellence and giving to kin. Today's word.
Your line: justice, excellence, kin. Today, give the one thing you chose to that relative, or set a time to do it, and do it a little better than you'd have to. Day four hundred fifty-four.

455.title: With wisdom
455.hook: invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good counsel, and argue in the best way (16:125)
455.howItsDone: Muslim teachers cite 16:125 as the guiding verse for da'wah, inviting others to Islam, and for interfaith conversation; many emphasize gentle speech and leaving guidance to God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, justice: the verse of the Friday sermon, with excellence and giving to kin. Did you give that relative something, or set a time to? Day four hundred fifty-five, the end of a week.

Somewhere right now there's a comment thread about religion that has gone on for two hundred replies. Nobody in it has changed their mind. Everyone in it has gotten a little meaner. Near the end of An-Nahl there's a verse about exactly this: how to talk about faith with people who don't share yours, or don't share your reading of it. It doesn't tell anyone to stay quiet. It tells them how to speak, and it names three tools.

Pickthall's translation of 16:125: "Call unto the way of thy Lord with wisdom and fair exhortation, and reason with them in the better way." Tool one: hikmah, wisdom. The root h-k-m has to do with holding something firm and judging well; the classical dictionaries list, from the same root, hakamah, the part of a horse's bridle that steers and restrains. Wisdom, in that picture, is knowing when to pull back. Saying the right thing at the right time to the right person, or saying nothing yet. Tool two: al-maw'izah al-hasanah, good counsel, the kind of advice that comes from someone who obviously cares about you. Tool three is the surprising one. Jadil: argue, debate. The verse doesn't forbid arguing. It says argue billati hiya ahsan, in the way that is best. Ahsan: the same root as ihsan from yesterday, excellence, doing something beautifully. So even a disagreement is supposed to be done well. Then the verse ends with a sentence that lowers the temperature of every argument: your Lord knows best who has strayed from His way, and He knows best who is guided. In the verse's terms, the speaker answers for the manner; the outcome is God's. Another verse, 29:46, makes the same point about the People of the Book: don't argue with them except in the best way. This week's verses were about gifts: countless favors, milk from between, the bee, and justice and excellence. Today the gifts turn into a way of talking: wise, kind, and, when it comes to arguing, beautiful.
screen: `HIKMAH: THE BRIDLE THAT STEERS.` · `GOOD COUNSEL, FROM SOMEONE WHO CARES.` · `ARGUE, BUT IN THE BEST WAY.` · `HE KNOWS BEST; THE RESULT ISN'T YOURS.` · then, large: `REASON WITH THEM IN THE BETTER WAY.`

segments.voice: The practice: disagree kindly, once. Sit, and bring to mind a disagreement you're in right now. It could be about faith, politics, or whose turn it is to do the dishes. Picture the other person's face. Now, slowly, find the strongest version of their point, the one they'd be glad to hear you say. Then picture yourself saying your own view in a way they could hear without bracing. Don't plan to win. Plan to speak well. The bell holds the time.
Hikmah. Wisdom, from a root about holding firm and judging well: the first tool for speaking about faith, before counsel and before argument. Today's word.
Your line: argue in the best way. Today, in one disagreement, say the other person's best point back to them before you make yours. Day four hundred fifty-five.

fork.setup: a friend mocks your faith in front of others, and you know you could win the argument. 16:125 has three tools. which comes first in the verse?
fork.reveal: wisdom comes first, then good counsel, then argument in the best way. and the verse ends by leaving the outcome to God.

original.note: Arabic: wisdom, from the root h-k-m, to hold firm and to judge.

trapdoor: what you thought: be wise when you talk about religion.
what it means: three tools in order, wisdom, good counsel, and argument done in the best way, with the result left to God.
what a scholar hears: h-k-m gives hakamah, part of a horse's bridle; ahsan in 'the better way' echoes ihsan in 16:90.
